title: Parking-Slot Gates for Overrun Villages
one_liner: Sell tiny hotspot villages and trailheads a plate-recognition parking and coach-slot reservation system whose price rises until arrivals fit a hard cap.
customer: Municipalities, mountain and coastal park authorities and private lot operators in places like Alpine lake villages, Dolomites passes, Cinque Terre-type towns and Croatian or Greek islands. Budgets are under EUR 50K, and they already own parking revenue.
problem: Venice's day-tripper fee reportedly did not cut numbers, because a small flat fee is dwarfed by trip cost. Open villages cannot install turnstiles, but almost every day visitor arrives by car, coach or shuttle. Those arrival modes are countable and enforceable, and nobody prices them dynamically.
solution: A cheap camera and plate-recognition kit plus a web app. Visitors reserve parking and coach slots at prices that rise with demand until the cap holds. Residents and overnight guests are exempt through a plate allow-list synced from hotels' check-in data. The cap becomes a subsidy for staying overnight.
why_now: Edge computer vision and plate recognition are now cheap. Record arrivals (1.52B international in 2025) and visible failures of flat fees have made mayors ready to try hard caps. Mount Fuji's 4,000/day cap plus fee shows caps are politically acceptable, and a few Alpine lakes already require reserved road access in peak season.
revenue_model: SaaS of EUR 300-900 per month per site, plus 3-5% of slot fees collected, plus a hardware lease.
non_obvious_insight: Price the arrival mode rather than the person. Cars and coaches are the physical valve for day-trip load, and exempting overnight guests turns a congestion rule into a booking incentive that local hotels will help sell.
first_30_days: Pick 3 villages that already have paid lots. Run a manual pilot with a reservation page and a phone-camera plate check by a local attendant, with no hardware. Sign private lot operators first, since they can decide fastest. Ask mayors for a summer 2027 pilot and a letter of support.

title: Employer-Backed Workforce Pell Program Packager
one_liner: Package 8-15 week, employer-guaranteed training programs that clear state approval and the 70% completion and 70% placement tests, paid per verified hire by the employers who need workers, with Pell covering tuition.
customer: Employers with chronic shortages (HVAC contractors, utilities and lineworker programs, hospitals for phlebotomy, CNA and sterile processing, machine shops, CDL trucking) paying per hire. Community and technical colleges are the Title IV-eligible partners.
problem: Workforce Pell (from 1 July 2026) opens Pell Grants to 150-599 clock-hour programs. A governor and state workforce board must approve each program as aligned to high-skill, high-wage, in-demand jobs, and programs must show at least 70% completion and 70% job placement plus a tuition-versus-earnings test. Colleges' continuing-ed divisions lack employer partnerships, placement tracking and approval paperwork skills. ED approved its first programs in mid-Sept 2026 (Nebraska, Texas, North Carolina) and 36 jurisdictions have an operating process.
solution: Act as a program packager and placement-assurance layer, not a tuition-share OPM, given the Title IV incentive-compensation rules. Steps: co-design the syllabus from employer job tasks; assemble the state approval dossier with employer letters and labor-market data; give the college cohort software covering employer offer commitments contingent on completion, completion nudges, and 180-day placement tracking via payroll and wage-record attestations; and bill employers per successful hire rather than per enrollment.
why_now: The program is only weeks old, states are just standing up approval processes, and the outcome thresholds will remove weak programs. Colleges need employer-tethered programs that can actually hit the 70/70 tests.
revenue_model: $2,000-$6,000 per hire from employers (well below typical 15-25% agency fees), $1-3k/month per college for cohort and placement software, and fixed fees for approval dossiers.
non_obvious_insight: The outcome test flips the customer. The college's real risk is the 70% placement rate, and only an employer that pre-commits to hire can guarantee it, so the payer is the employer rather than the student or school. Pell effectively becomes a federal training subsidy for whichever employers organize demand first.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a live approval process and shortages (Texas, North Carolina or Nebraska) and one sector such as HVAC, lineworker or sterile processing. Collect 5 employer hiring commitments and co-apply with 1-2 community colleges for a 10-week program. Run a non-Pell pilot cohort while approval is pending to test placement, and have counsel review the incentive-compensation boundary.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Public Buyers
angle: Pairing 2: Reshoring, tariffs & automation x Government / defense / municipal
one_liner: A contingency-fee audit that finds 'tariff surcharge' line items on city, school-district, transit and university purchase orders and recovers the share vendors are now being refunded after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs.
customer: County and city finance departments, school districts, transit agencies, public universities and public hospitals. They pay 20-30% of dollars recovered and nothing upfront.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. Roughly 330,000 importers paid about $166B, and as of July only about $86B had been repaid, so about $80B remained outstanding. Refunds go to the importer of record, not to the public buyers who paid vendor surcharges (one machine-shop supplier surcharge was 2.7%). Small importers and delivered-duty-unpaid shipments, including many university and hospital equipment imports, are likely to go unclaimed. Brokers are paid per entry and have no reason to chase this.
solution: Step 1: mine open-checkbook portals to rank vendors in tariff-exposed categories (school buses, HVAC, lab equipment, IT, furniture, playgrounds) and file public-records requests for their invoices to find surcharge lines. Step 2: send standardized pass-through refund claims and negotiate credit memos where the contract or surcharge language supports it. Step 3: where the public entity was itself importer of record (DDU), file its own refund claims. A dashboard tracks vendor refund status and the client's recovered dollars.
why_now: Refunds are flowing in phases now, with liquidated-entry and AD/CVD cases coming later, so vendor cash is fresh but memory of surcharges will fade. Claim deadlines and statutes of limitation close within 12-18 months. Public entities are under budget pressure and readily accept no-cost recovery audits, as with utility-bill and sales-tax audits.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered dollars, with a lower fee on refunds recovered by filing as importer of record. The same platform later runs recurring price-escalation monitoring for a subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The money sits with a party who has no incentive to hand it over, while the party who bore the cost has unusual leverage: public buyers can demand transparency, make supplier performance part of the record, and threaten future award eligibility. Public procurement contracts and open-checkbook data make targets findable without any client cooperation.
first_30_days: Pull open-checkbook data for 3 states, file about 30 public-records requests for surcharge invoices, and have counsel review a standard claim letter. Cold-email 20 finance directors with a personalized 'you likely overpaid $X to Vendor Y' one-pager and sign two pilots on contingency.

title: Reef Mixtapes for Oyster Hatcheries and Reefs
one_liner: Underwater speakers and a licensed library of healthy-reef soundscapes that lure oyster larvae to settle in hatchery tanks and restoration sites.
customer: Oyster hatcheries and remote-setting operations, oyster farmers, and restoration NGOs and state shellfish agencies such as those running large reef programs.
problem: Larval settlement is a costly bottleneck: eyed larvae are expensive to raise and many fail to set on cultch. Restoration reefs built on bare bottom get poor recruitment because they are silent, while healthy reefs act like acoustic beacons.
solution: A plug-in kit of a waterproof speaker, a controller and a subscription to species- and region-specific reef sound libraries recorded on healthy local reefs (snapping-shrimp crackle in the 1.5-20 kHz range). It ships with a built-in split-tank A/B protocol so any hatchery can measure the settlement gain in a week. Restoration clients can pay per acre on measured recruitment. Later products: playback buoys and acoustic tuning per species.
why_now: The science is now credible and publicised. Lab playbacks showed more oyster settlement under reef sound than under soft-bottom sound or silence (Lillis et al., PLOS ONE 2013), and later work reported large increases. In July 2026 WHOI, with The Nature Conservancy Massachusetts and shellfish constables, began a two-year effort to build a 'New England mixtape' for farmers and restorers. Rugged hydrophones and speakers are cheap. Nobody has yet packaged this for commerce.
revenue_model: Hardware kit at roughly $600-1,500, a library subscription of $50-150 per month per site, and performance-based restoration contracts (for example a share of measured settlement gains or per-acre fees). Longer term, license the sound and response dataset to acoustic-restoration players.
non_obvious_insight: Larvae navigate by ear, and degraded reefs are literally silent, so sound is a cheap cue you can sell. The defensible asset is the proprietary library of local recordings plus the settlement-response data by species and region. Commercial-hatchery effect sizes are still unproven, so the honest first product is the A/B testing rig and pay-on-results pricing, which turns scientific uncertainty into the sales pitch.
first_30_days: Buy two hydrophones and two speakers. Get three small hatcheries to run split-tank A/B settlement counts with a simple protocol, and record one healthy reef per region. Publish the first results and convert the hatcheries with the strongest lift into paying $1,500 kits.

title: Knowledge Trusts That Pay Heirs From AI Licensing
angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x Death, estates and the great wealth transfer
one_liner: A fiduciary licensing shop that records a retiring or terminally ill master practitioner's judgment, holds the rights in an estate-friendly trust, sells non-exclusive licenses to AI buyers, and pays royalties to the expert and later the heirs.
customer: Two payers. First, employers and trade associations with an irreplaceable expert aged 62-75 about to retire, who pay for a knowledge-capture sprint. Second, AI labs, vertical AI vendors and professional-training firms that license the corpus. Beneficiaries are the expert and heirs. Channel: estate attorneys and wealth managers, who want an heir-engagement hook (Cerulli says 89% of firms treat family meetings as essential).
problem: The scarcest input for AI is long-tail, high-stakes tacit judgment (how a 40-year surety underwriter smells a bad bond, how a master electrician diagnoses an odd fault). It sits in the heads of people near retirement or death. Hourly expert-gig marketplaces pay by the hour with no royalties. They rarely reach 65+ specialists, and nobody structures who owns the recordings, annotations or persona rights after death, so it all falls into probate limbo. Meanwhile 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are about 19% below trend (Stanford) and have no path to learn from these people.
solution: 1) Structured elicitation: 30-40 hours of rubric-guided sessions (case walk-throughs, 'what would you do and why not that', annotated redacted real work). Junior apprentice-interviewers from the same field, meaning recent grads or displaced mid-career people, run them. They are paid and earn a verifiable co-credit. 2) Rights go into a knowledge trust drafted with the client's estate attorney: consent controls, approved-buyer list, sunset dates, and no voice, likeness or persona cloning unless explicitly opted in. 3) Non-exclusive licensing of the corpus to labs and enterprise vendors. Royalties go to the expert while alive and to heirs afterward.
why_now: Mercor's $10B valuation (Oct 2025) and reported ~$2B gross run-rate (Jun 2026, lower-tier source, verify) proved frontier labs pay heavily for expert judgment, while contractors complain about pay and lack of protection. Roughly 4M Americans turn 65 each year, and Cerulli projects $124T in transfers through 2048. Postmortem publicity and digital-replica laws are maturing (for example California's 70-year postmortem term). The junior hiring freeze creates a cheap, motivated interviewer pool.
revenue_model: Employer-funded capture sprints at $15-40K per expert (a succession-planning budget line). License revenue share, roughly 40% to expert/estate, 40% to us, 20% to an apprentice pool. Trust administration fee of about 1% of royalties per year. Optional per-client fee from advisors or attorneys who bundle it into estate plans.
non_obvious_insight: The estate, not the living person, is the natural licensor of a lifetime of judgment. Postmortem and IP rights live in probate, and royalty streams fit inheritance planning better than hourly gigs do. Retirees who would never take a gig will happily fund grandchildren with a legacy asset. The demand is a fixed-time resource (a retirement wave) that becomes unavailable once experts are gone.
first_30_days: Pick two narrow, lab-relevant, high-liability trades (for example construction surety adjusters and commercial roofing estimators). Recruit 8-10 retiring experts via trade-association newsletters and five friendly estate attorneys. Pitch each expert's employer a $20K 'retirement capture sprint' as the cash-generating wedge, with licensing rights reserved for the expert's trust. Hire 3 laid-off or junior domain grads as interviewers. Run two pilots. Send redacted sample corpora to 10 human-data teams and vertical AI startups to pre-sell licenses.

title: The Weekly Mail Box for Mom
one_liner: A prepaid return envelope where a parent drops all her mail. It gets scanned, triaged, shredded, and turned into a 'what needs doing' digest for her adult child.
customer: Adult children aged 45-62 with a parent 75+ living alone, often 100+ miles away. Secondary customers are daily money managers, professional fiduciaries and elder-law firms who currently collect and read mail by hand.
problem: Paper mail is where scams (fake invoices, 'prize fees', Medicare plan pitches), real bills and the notices that cost money arrive: property-tax exemption renewals, Part D changes, IRS notices, Medicaid paperwork. Kids discover the unopened shoebox at Thanksgiving. USPS Informed Delivery shows only the exterior of some letter-size mail. Parents refuse apps, dashboards and shared passwords because that feels like surrender.
solution: A weekly pre-addressed return flat that the parent fills with the whole pile, with no sorting. The team scans it, uses AI to classify and extract sender, amount, due date and required action, flags likely scams (any 'send a check to claim your prize' letter), and calls or texts the parent for urgent items ('Do you want the water bill paid?'). The child gets a weekly digest and a dashboard. Originals are shredded or returned monthly, per the parent's choice. Over time it builds the 'where everything is' paper trail that estates need: accounts, policies, pensions and annuities.
why_now: Cheap, accurate AI document extraction only became affordable at consumer prices in the last two years. Treasury phased out paper checks on Sept 30, 2025, and agencies are pushing digital, while seniors still get paper notices. Older-adult scam losses run in the billions per year (FTC). Medicare open enrollment begins Oct 15, so the mailer flood is imminent.
revenue_model: $49/month per household (about $14 in postage, scanning and AI, for roughly 70% gross margin). $25 per household per month wholesale for daily money managers and fiduciaries. Optional $149 one-time 'estate paper trail' report.
non_obvious_insight: Seniors will turn down every dashboard, but they will hand over an envelope pile happily, because mailing is a ritual they own. The pile is the real system of record for a widow's finances. Scam checks and wire requests are usually triggered by letters, so scanning the inside of the envelope catches what exterior-only tools cannot. Children do not want passwords either. They want to know what to pay.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 households in one metro through caregiver Facebook groups, local AARP caregiver meetings and elder-law attorneys. Run it manually with a $500 duplex scanner, an AI extraction pipeline and a retired teacher doing quality checks. Charge from day one. Track 'catches' (scams intercepted, missed notices found) and publish them. Then pitch daily money managers.

title: Calibration Target Network for Earth-Observation Startups
one_liner: Networked ground calibration targets that issue overpass-synchronized calibration certificates for EO satellites.
customer: EO and SAR constellation operators, analytics firms selling certified measurements (insurance, methane, deforestation), and government agencies.
problem: Every new imaging satellite needs geometric and radiometric calibration, mostly done ad hoc. As EO output becomes regulated evidence, buyers ask who certified the sensor, and no third party provides traceable, on-demand ground truth.
solution: Deploy SAR corner reflectors, spectral tarps and instrumented sites (GPS, weather, irradiance) at a handful of stable locations. Automatically log each satellite overpass and issue a calibration certificate. Offer custom validation sites and controlled-release campaigns for customers.
why_now: The EO sector is mature and government-anchored (Planet's large contracts and Pelican production doubling per the briefing). Regulated uses raise demand for traceability. Many new SAR and hyperspectral entrants launch each year.
revenue_model: $30-150k per year per constellation. Project fees for custom validation sites. Certificates sold to analytics customers.
non_obvious_insight: As EO becomes evidence, the bottleneck is ground presence synchronized with overpasses, not more data.
first_30_days: Pick two well-known desert sites and place a first set of low-cost reflectors and tarps. Offer free certificates to three SAR and optical startups in return for testimonials, and ask for paid annual plans after the first quarter.

title: Accessible Council Packets Pipeline
one_liner: An automated pipeline that makes every agenda packet, staff report and PDF a city publishes accessible on arrival, ahead of the ADA Title II deadline.
customer: City and county clerks and IT directors in jurisdictions above 50,000 residents (deadline April 26, 2027), then smaller ones (2028).
problem: Cities publish thousands of legacy PDFs, scanned minutes and meeting packets that fail web accessibility rules. Manual remediation costs $3-10 per page and lawsuits are coming. Staffing is thin, and the deadline is fixed.
solution: Connect to the city's agenda-management and document repository, auto-remediate PDFs (tags, reading order, alt text, tables), route low-confidence pages to human reviewers, and enforce accessible-by-default templates for future documents. Provide the compliance log a city attorney can cite.
why_now: ADA Title II rules set April 2027 for larger jurisdictions and 2028 for smaller ones. GenAI makes remediation of complex documents cheap enough to price against manual work.
revenue_model: $15-80K per year per city depending on volume, plus a backlog cleanup fee ($20-100K one-time).
non_obvious_insight: The recurring stream of new weekly agenda packets, not the legacy backlog, is the durable business. Ship the pipeline at the moment of publishing rather than a one-time remediation project.
first_30_days: Scrape 20 city websites and score their accessibility publicly. Offer free packet remediation for the next council meeting to 5 clerks. Convert on the backlog cleanup quote.

title: Fire-Line Readiness Passport for Contract Wildfire Crews
one_liner: A qualifications, equipment-inspection and shift-ticket system for private wildland fire engine and crew owners, built so they are never rejected at check-in or paid late.
customer: Owners of private wildland fire engines, hand crews and water tenders contracted by federal and state agencies (the national association alone represents 300+ contractors). A single rig or crew can gross six figures in a season.
problem: Contract fire resources are dispatched from agency lists and must show current qualifications, red cards, fitness tests, insurance, vehicle and pump inspections and correct rate documentation. A missing or expired item gets the rig rejected or sent home at check-in. Payment then depends on shift tickets being filled out and reconciled correctly. Errors mean holds and weeks of waiting while the owner fronts payroll, fuel and insurance. Most operators run this on paper and text messages.
solution: A mobile passport per crew member and rig. It tracks qualification and training expiry, physical and medical dates, insurance certificates and equipment checklists against the specific contract's rules. It flags what will fail at check-in, generates GPS-and-time-stamped shift tickets in agency format with automated checks against contract rates, and packages payment documents. Later it adds accelerated payment.
why_now: Agencies are leaning heavily on contractors, the national Type 2-IA crew contract cycle continues through 2026-27, and the wildfire workforce and pay rules are shifting. It is late September, so the off-season sales window for 2027 contracts is open and there is time to build an MVP before next season.
revenue_model: $150-400 per engine or crew per month. A 1-2% fee on accelerated payment advances against verified, error-free packets, once the record system proves low rejection rates. Insurance and training referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: In fire contracting, the paperwork is the collateral. The rig-days lost to rejection and the payment delays from ticket errors are the real costs. A system that pre-validates packets against the contract's own rules is trusted by agencies, insurers and factoring companies alike, so it can become the data layer for everything financial in the niche. The market looks small (roughly a thousand firms), but each firm has an unusually high willingness to pay.
first_30_days: Join the national contractor association's conversations and contact owners on state preseason contract lists in Oregon, Idaho, Montana and California. Offer a $750-1,500 'pre-season readiness audit' per rig, mapping each contract's checklist. Use the audits to design the MVP. Sell subscriptions from February for the 2027 season.

title: Purpose-Locked Guardian Funds for Pets
angle: Finance (household finance, programmable money, trusts) x Pets & animal health
one_liner: A pre-funded account that pays a named pet guardian through a card locked to vet and pet spending when the owner dies or is hospitalized.
customer: Adults 55+ and single owners with dogs or cats, sold through estate-planning attorneys, hospice and palliative social workers, hospital discharge planners and senior-living communities. The named guardian is the user.
problem: When owners die, are hospitalized or enter care, pets often become shelter intakes. Pet trusts cost $1,500-3,000 in legal fees and rely on trust that money reaches the animal. An informal promise to a niece falls apart when she faces a $4,000 vet bill, and a dog's lifetime cost is about $34K. Pets are also a documented reason some older adults delay hospital care.
solution: A low-fee guardian account funded by lump sum, monthly premium or life-insurance beneficiary designation. On a verified trigger (death certificate, or a social worker's hospital admission attestation) the guardian receives a purpose-locked card restricted by merchant category to vet, food and boarding, plus a monthly stipend. A records vault carries vet history. A vetted foster network is the fallback if the guardian declines. Leftovers go to heirs or a named charity.
why_now: Card-issuing and BaaS APIs make purpose-restricted cards cheap. Vet costs have risen much faster than general prices, so guardianship is a real financial obligation. The large pandemic-era adoption cohort is aging, and more older adults live alone. Stablecoin-era interest in programmable, purpose-bound money has made restricted-use funds a familiar concept.
revenue_model: $149-199 setup fee, about 1.5% annual administration fee on balances, card interchange, and attorney or hospice referral fees. Insurers and employers may later fund it as a rider.
non_obvious_insight: The legal trust is not the product. The product is a guarantee that money reaches the animal and that a stranger can act fast, and purpose-locked spending is what delivers it. This is one of the few pet products where the buyer is not the beneficiary, so trust and distribution channels matter more than price.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 estate-planning attorneys and 3 hospice or palliative-care social-work teams in one metro. Sell a $149 'pet guardian plan' with a pooled trust via a licensed trust-company partner and a sponsor-bank card. Target 30 funded accounts of $1,000-3,000 each in the first quarter.

title: Grandschools: Microschools Inside Senior Communities
one_liner: Turnkey K-8 microschools hosted in senior-living and 55+ communities, with residents as mentors and tuition funded by ESAs and scholarship credits.
customer: Senior-living operators and 55+ communities (pay a program fee for engagement and occupancy marketing); families paying tuition, ESA or scholarship dollars; retired professionals as mentors.
problem: More than 1,000 public schools closed in 2025-26, families are being displaced, and microschools struggle to find trusted adults (at Alpha School two-thirds of guides lack teaching credentials). Senior communities struggle with purpose-driven programming and occupancy. Each side has the resource the other lacks.
solution: A franchise-lite pilot model of 12-24 kids, 1 lead guide and 6-10 resident 'grand-mentors' (retired engineers, teachers, nurses) running project blocks, sharing dining, garden and library space. A standard playbook covers background checks, safeguarding, insurance, private-school registration and a mentor-hour ledger. Enrollment through ESA and SGO scholarships.
why_now: The demographic cliff in kids meets the aging peak. Scholarship credits and ESAs from 2027 make tuition viable for middle-income families, and the microschool guide shortage is acute.
revenue_model: $6-9k per child in tuition or ESA funds; operator program fee of $1-2k a month (or free space); licensing and playbook fees when replicating.
non_obvious_insight: The two halves of the demographic shift are each other's missing input: shrinking youth cohorts leave surplus buildings, growing elderly cohorts hold surplus expertise, and aging-services operators have engagement budgets that schools have never tapped.
first_30_days: Approach 10 independent-living communities in one metro that have on-site classrooms and sign one. Recruit 10 families from closed-school parent groups and a certified guide. Launch a 'Fridays' pilot before a full schedule. Confirm state private-school registration and insurance first.

title: Install-and-Map Crew for Crowdfunded Yard Robots
one_liner: A local white-glove setup and seasonal-care service for the $4-5K yard robots that Kickstarter backers are buying and struggling to get working.
customer: Owners of $2,200-$5,500 crowdfunded or prosumer yard robots (Yarbo M and similar): affluent suburban homeowners with 0.5-2 acres, seniors who cannot lift a 200 lb unit, and small landscaping and snow-removal firms. Payer is the homeowner or firm, with an installer-referral fee from manufacturers or resellers as a later option.
problem: Big-ticket crowdfunded robots ship as a Shenzhen-supported product that takes multiple weekends to set up: RTK antenna placement, GPS calibration, yard mapping, no-go zones, firmware chasing. It weighs about 200 lb, and owners report escalations without resolution from a China-based support team.
solution: A certified two-person install crew that does a one-visit RTK site survey (satellite-visibility check, antenna mounting), lifts and assembles the unit, maps the yard, sets zones and snow paths, and hands off with a 30-day check-in. Add a $19/mo seasonal-care plan covering firmware updates, blade and attachment swaps, and pre-winter snow-blower setup. Start with Yarbo, then extend to other $3K+ crowdfunded home robots and ultra-short-throw laser projectors (5,260 backers took the $2,999 XGIMI tier).
why_now: Yarbo M backers were told to expect delivery from August 2026, and snow-blower-module backers ship mid-November, right before the season the module exists for. That gives a hard deadline in autumn 2026. Wire-free RTK robots are only now cheap enough for homeowners, and the seniors and heavy-yard buyers who most need help are exactly the ones who cannot self-install.
revenue_model: $399-$799 per install visit (higher for wooded or complex lots), $19/mo or $149/yr seasonal-care plan, and $99-$199 per attachment swap or spring/fall visit. Optional B2B contracts for landscapers converting to robot fleets.
non_obvious_insight: The Kickstarter tech median pledge is $194, but this robot's backers average over $4,000 each ($3,158,140 from 751 backers, https://www.gizmocrowd.com/post/yarbo-m-yard-robot). At that price the buyer is effectively a serviced-equipment customer, not a gadget hobbyist. Hands-on reviews say setup took multiple weekends, the unit weighs about 200 lb (owners "could not have set the unit up alone"), GPS struggles under tree cover, support runs from China with East Coast friction, and the maker declined Home Assistant API access in March 2025 (https://seekandscore.com/yarbo-review/). Crowdfunded hardware makers optimise for shipping units, not last-mile success, so the installer layer is unowned. It is a local-services business with software-like repeat revenue.
first_30_days: Read public Kickstarter and Yarbo forum comments to find backers in snow-belt ZIP codes, and post in the Yarbo owner communities offering a founding-customer $299 install. Recruit 2-3 landscapers or handymen who already own a truck and lift gear. Run 5 paid installs on your own or friends' properties to write a mapping and RTK-survey checklist, then film one before/after case study. Book 15-20 installs timed to the November snow-blower shipments and sign one landscaping firm to a pilot contract.

title: Credit Ratings and Insurance for Virtual Power Plants
one_liner: A neutral firmness rating plus a parametric shortfall policy, so hyperscalers and utilities can buy VPP megawatts they can actually count.
customer: VPP operators and installers (pay for the rating), hyperscalers and utilities buying capacity (subscribe to reports), and reinsurers and MGAs (take the risk and pay a fronting fee).
problem: Sunrun, Tesla and Renew Home announced 16.8 GW of 'capacity-as-a-service' for data centers with no disclosed pricing, metering or verification standard. A 580 MW dispatch from 140k batteries on Sept 9 proves the tech works, but one event is not firm capacity. Buyers under bring-your-own-capacity rules need MW they can legally rely on.
solution: Publish a methodology that works like ELCC for distributed fleets: fleet-level P50/P90 availability by season and hour from attested device telemetry, with letter-grade tiers. Add a parametric policy, underwritten by a partner MGA or reinsurer, that pays the buyer if delivered MW falls below rated MW in a dispatch event. Start with public data from the ERCOT ADER pilot and California's DSGS program.
why_now: Hyperscaler-VPP deals, PJM's curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule and real dispatch events like Sept 9 mean there is finally enough event data to rate fleets.
revenue_model: $50-250k a year per fleet rated, subscriptions from buyers, and a fee or premium share on the insurance wrap.
non_obvious_insight: The VPP industry thinks its hard problem is enrollment. The buyer's hard problem is trust. Hyperscalers only pay for 'firm' if a third party is on the hook. Ratings plus insurance turn dispatch volatility into a financial product, and the standard-setter collects a toll on every MW sold.
first_30_days: Publish an unsolicited scorecard of public ERCOT ADER and California DSGS dispatch performance. Offer 15 VPP operators a free confidential rating in exchange for telemetry. Sound out two MGAs or reinsurers on parametric structure. Pre-sell a rating to one aggregator that is already pitching hyperscalers.

title: Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions
one_liner: Track carriers' filed AI exclusions and tell brokers, 90 days before renewal, which clients just lost AI coverage, then place the affirmative buy-back.
customer: Independent agencies and regional brokers (10-200 staff) with commercial books, their E&O carriers, and MGAs.
problem: Since January 2026 ISO-style generative-AI endorsements (CG 40 47 and CG 40 48) and far broader carrier forms, such as W. R. Berkley's 'absolute' AI exclusion, are attached at renewal, often buried. Clients use AI in ways they never disclosed. Brokers carry E&O exposure for failing to warn, and no tool maps which of a broker's 300 clients face AI exclusions or what AI each client actually uses.
solution: A rate and form filing scraper (public SERFF filing access) plus an endorsement parser that normalises exclusion breadth: gen-AI only versus any AI, bodily injury versus advertising injury, vendor-supplied AI. It feeds a renewal calendar imported from agency-management CSVs. A 12-question client AI-use questionnaire, optionally backed by an SSO or expense-report scan for AI tools. Output is a one-page 'AI coverage gap letter' plus a list of affirmative AI markets for placement.
why_now: 1 Jan 2027 renewals are the first big cycle after the Verisk endorsements became available, and AIG, Great American and Berkley filings landed through 2026. Affirmative AI capacity now exists (Armilla via Lloyd's, AIUC, Munich Re aiSure), so a gap and its fix can be sold together.
revenue_model: $250-800 per month per agency, $150-600 per gap letter for non-subscribers, 10-15% commission on affirmative cover placed, and $2-5k per month filing-intelligence subscriptions for MGAs and carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is triggered by their own E&O fear, not curiosity about AI. The filings are public but unreadable, so the moat is a normalised exclusion database nobody at a brokerage has time to build. Silent AI cuts both ways: an unexcluded policy is a reason to ask for affirmative cover, so the gap letter also works as a sales tool for the broker.
first_30_days: Scrape SERFF filings in five large states and build the tracker. Start a free weekly 'AI exclusion tracker' newsletter aimed at 500 brokers. Offer 10 agencies a $500 concierge gap audit on their five biggest accounts. Sign one affirmative-AI MGA for placement referrals.

title: Vacancy-Permit Kit for Half-Empty Offices
one_liner: A sensor and inspection package that keeps half-empty office buildings insurable and safe during the 12-36 months of limbo before resolution.
customer: Special servicers, receivers and owners of office buildings under roughly 31% occupancy or with dark floors, plus lender-placed insurance managers.
problem: Many standard commercial property forms treat a building as vacant unless about 31% of its area is leased and in use, and after 60 days of vacancy exclude vandalism, water damage, theft and glass while cutting other payouts (buildings under renovation are exempt). Meanwhile stagnant plumbing raises Legionella risk, HVAC is wasted, and squatters and fire watch add cost. About 15.7% of office CMBS is in special servicing, and resolutions take years.
solution: Flow and temperature sensors with automated flush valves, HVAC setback tied to the building system, AI door and intrusion cameras and documented monthly inspections. Packaged as evidence for a vacancy permit or protective-safeguards endorsement and as reporting to servicers, installed only on dark floors.
why_now: Distress is at record levels with long resolutions, property insurance is costly and restrictive, and IoT and video analytics are cheap.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.30 per sf per year subscription plus $1-3 per sf install, with referral fees from commercial insurance brokers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is writing about conversion, but nobody services the limbo period where value leaks through insurance denials and stagnant water. A few dollars of sensors can be cheaper than one uninsured water loss.
first_30_days: Partner with two commercial brokers who place vacant-building coverage. Pilot at two receiver-owned buildings for about $5K each. Ask an insurer to accept the protocol in writing.

title: Fake-Citation Triage for Defendants Facing Pro Se Filings
one_liner: A same-day report showing which citations in an opposing pro se filing are fake, misquoted or overruled, formatted as a court-ready exhibit for a motion to strike or for sanctions.
customer: Repeat defendants that get flooded with self-represented suits: landlord and property-management litigation groups, employment-defense boutiques, university and hospital counsel, insurer claims-litigation units, debt servicers, city attorney offices and municipal risk pools. Paid by the litigation budget owner.
problem: Charlotin's database holds about 2,095 AI-hallucination cases as of 28 Sep 2026, and 1,208 (58%) involve pro se litigants versus 829 involving lawyers. Pro se filers are immune to bar discipline, sanctions ($1,750 to $23,222) are slow and rare, and the defendant pays $300-600/hour of associate time to hand-check dozens of cites. Every hallucination-checker on the market is pitched to the lawyer who erred.
solution: Drag-and-drop a PDF. The tool extracts citations (open-source eyecite plus CourtListener), resolves each one, and flags nonexistent cases, quotes that do not appear in the opinion, wrong court or year, and negative treatment. Output is a two-page 'Citation Defect Declaration' plus a draft paragraph for a motion to strike or a Rule 11-type motion. Phase two hooks into the e-service email inbox so every incoming filing is screened automatically.
why_now: The volume of fabricated-citation filings is now measured in the thousands and judges have seen enough to act on them. Open case-law data (CourtListener) is now good enough that OpenAI built Astra for Law on it (17 Sep 2026), so the verification corpus is cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: $49-149 per filing report self-serve, or $1,500-5,000/month flat for repeat defendants with inbox integration. Upsell is drafting of the sanctions or strike motion at a fixed fee.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer everyone targets (the erring lawyer) has a small budget and an embarrassment problem. The money and standing sit with the counterparty, who pays hourly to verify someone else's junk and is the only actor who can turn a bad cite into leverage (strike, fee-shifting, vexatious-litigant designation).
first_30_days: Build on eyecite and the CourtListener API, then benchmark accuracy on 100 known cases from the Charlotin database as ground truth. Cold-email 30 landlord-tenant and employment-defense firms and 10 municipal risk pools, offering 10 free reports in exchange for permission to attach a report to a filing. Charge $99 per report after that and aim for 3-5 recurring accounts.

title: Dialysis Chair-Fill Rides Paid Per Completed Treatment
one_liner: A dedicated, route-based ride service for dialysis patients (same driver, same van loop, three times a week) priced per treatment completed instead of per trip, sold to the clinics and risk-bearing kidney-care companies that lose money on every missed session.
customer: Independent dialysis clinic groups and mid-sized operators worried about chair utilization, plus value-based kidney-care companies and Medicare Advantage ESRD plans that carry the hospitalization cost when a patient misses treatment.
problem: Medicaid non-emergency transport is a low-margin, hated business: pooled dispatch, late or missed pickups, and one-off rides for patients who actually have 156 predictable trips a year. The largest broker, ModivCare, went through Chapter 11 in 2025, so states and payers are unhappy with the incumbent. Meanwhile a missed dialysis session is expensive: in one study about 5% of patients were hospitalized within two days of a missed appointment versus 1.2% of those who attended. Medicare pays the clinic a bundled rate of about $282 per treatment in 2026, so every no-show is lost revenue, an idle chair and staff, and a sicker patient.
solution: Run dialysis like a bus route. Batch patients by chair shift and neighborhood, fix pickup windows, and assign dedicated driver-and-vehicle pairs so the patient sees the same person every time. Add SMS check-in, a same-day fallback ride through a taxi or rideshare partner, and a no-show guarantee. Report completed-treatment rates to the clinic weekly. Price by completed treatment (a round trip in the tens of dollars against roughly $280 of chair revenue), with an upside share for a lower missed-session rate. Structure it inside the Anti-Kickback local-transportation safe harbor, or bill risk-bearing plans and kidney-care companies directly, and confirm that with health-care counsel before launch.
why_now: ModivCare's bankruptcy and its emergence at the end of 2025 left NEMT contracts in flux and states re-examining brokers. CMS's kidney care models and Medicare Advantage special-needs plans are pushing risk onto companies that now feel every hospital day. Federal Medicaid cuts mean clinics and plans need cheaper ways to protect revenue rather than more benefits.
revenue_model: Fee per completed treatment (about $45-$75 round trip depending on wheelchair mix), with a bonus tied to reducing the clinic's missed-treatment rate. Second line: chemo and radiation patients on the same route logic.
non_obvious_insight: A dialysis chair is perishable inventory, like an airline seat, and the ride is a $50 cost that protects a $280 seat-day and a threefold hospitalization risk. NEMT is a terrible business because it treats a predictable, recurring, high-stakes patient as a random one-off trip. Treat those patients as a subscription route and the economics flip from a race to the bottom on price per mile to a premium on reliability.
first_30_days: Sell one independent operator with 3-5 clinics in one metro on a 60-day pilot covering 15-20 patients. Use two leased accessible vans, or subcontract a local NEMT operator, and two salaried drivers. Get the clinic's baseline missed-treatment rate from its own records and agree the target in writing before starting. Charge per completed treatment from day one, then take the data to a kidney-care company or MA plan for a larger contract.

title: Remote Athletic Trainer Coverage for Rural Schools
one_liner: A subscription sideline triage line, protocol library and documentation service that stretches one licensed athletic trainer across many schools.
customer: Rural and small school districts, state athletic associations and school risk pools paying $6-20k per school per season.
problem: NATA-cited figures show about 41 percent of Kansas schools and 68 percent of Oklahoma schools lack an athletic trainer, only about a third of Arkansas schools have one, and Massachusetts does not require one (Boston Globe, September 28, 2026). Coaches make return-to-play calls and handle concussions, heat and cardiac emergencies ad hoc, and districts carry the liability.
solution: Licensed ATs run a game-time line where coaches call or video-chat for triage; ATs guide return-to-play, do next-day follow-ups, document per state concussion law, and supply emergency action plans and coach training. Optional phase two: AT review of clips from schools' existing AI cameras.
why_now: 2026 shortage coverage keeps escalating, legislatures are debating mandates, and schools already own cheap AI cameras and video-call tools.
revenue_model: $6-20k per school per season, district-wide contracts, risk-pool discounts, and per-event tournament coverage fees.
non_obvious_insight: Training more ATs will not fix this within five years; extending each AT's reach 5-10x will. School insurers and risk pools care about concussion litigation and will subsidize it, so it is sold as liability reduction rather than healthcare.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 part-time or retired ATs licensed in one state, pitch 10 districts on a 4-week football-season pilot at $2.5k, and pitch that state's school risk pool on co-funding.

title: Independent Inspections for AI-Built Software
one_liner: A third-party inspection-and-certificate service, staffed by displaced senior engineers, that tells buyers, lenders and insurers what is really inside AI-generated apps before money changes hands.
customer: Buyers of micro-SaaS and small apps on acquisition marketplaces (deals $20k-$2M), SMBs whose apps were built by vibe-coding freelancers, seed investors doing diligence and lenders financing software purchases.
problem: Insiders say AI made software cheap, but the cost moved to trust. Marketplaces are filling with prompt-built products of unknown security, licensing and maintainability, and misconfigured database rules in AI-generated apps have been reported. Traditional code audits cost $10-50k and take weeks. Meanwhile senior devs sit unemployed for many months.
solution: A fixed-price 48-hour 'app inspection': automated scans (secrets, dependency licences, database access rules, auth and PII flows) plus a 2-4 hour senior human review. The output is a standardised graded report like a home-inspection report, with repair-cost estimates and a maintainability score. Inspectors are paid $500-900 each, and an optional badge can be accepted by escrow agents.
why_now: The vibe-coding boom in 2025-26 flooded acquisition marketplaces with AI-built listings, agentic scanners make the first pass nearly free, and unemployed senior engineers are abundant.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per inspection at 40-50% gross margin, recurring contracts with portfolio buyers, and referral fees from repair shops.
non_obvious_insight: When production cost collapses, value shifts to attestation. Every asset that became cheap to produce (1970s housing, used cars, diamonds) spawned an independent inspector class. Nobody has yet set the trusted standard for AI-built software, and the inspectors' seniority is the moat, the same people the market calls redundant.
first_30_days: Offer discounted $500 inspections in acquisition-marketplace buyer forums and Indie Hackers. Recruit 6 laid-off senior engineers and run 10 inspections on live listings. Publish anonymised findings ('7 of 10 exposed user data') and sign one escrow or broker referral partner.

title: DNA-Certified Coral Frag Registry
one_liner: A genotype registry where reef breeders register mother colonies and buyers verify that a $500 frag is genuinely the named morph.
customer: Coral breeders and vendors, frag-swap organizers, high-end reef hobbyists and aquarium auction sites.
problem: Frags are clones, so one genotype circulates under multiple names and different colonies share a name. Studies of aquarium-trade corals show named morphs and common names are messy, and DNA barcodes do not resolve Acropora from the trade. High-value morphs sell for hundreds to thousands of dollars with no provenance.
solution: Genotype tissue clippings with low-cost SNP or amplicon panels through a partner lab. Breeders register mother genotypes with their signature, buyers mail a clipping (~$40) for a match, vendors display a 'DNA-verified' badge, and a searchable registry prevents duplicate naming and supports lineage and royalty claims.
why_now: Cheap sequencing and ML-based genotype calling make per-sample cost low enough for hobbyists. The research gap between barcodes and genotype identification is now documented.
revenue_model: $40 per verification, $99 breeder registration, a $29/month vendor badge subscription, and royalties on licensed morphs.
non_obvious_insight: In clonal organisms the genotype is the product, yet the market prices names, which are marketing. The first to make genotype searchable creates something like a plant-variety registry, which breeders will fund because it protects their premium. Expect challenges from species-specific panels, symbiont DNA and shipping rules.
first_30_days: Partner with a genomics lab. Test 100 frags from 5 well-known vendors' same-name corals for free and publish any duplicate genotypes sold under multiple names in reefing forums. Sell the first 300 paid tests.
